prompt: In an unweighted graph, which traversal finds the path with the fewest edges from a source to every reachable vertex?
options: Depth-first search
Topological sort
Inorder traversal
Breadth-first search
explanation: BFS explores vertices in order of their edge distance from the source, so the first path it finds to each vertex has the fewest edges.

prompt: Which data structure does depth-first search use, explicitly or via recursion?
options: A queue
A stack
A priority queue
A hash set only
explanation: DFS follows last-in, first-out order: the call stack (or an explicit stack) remembers where to backtrack.

prompt: What is the space complexity of an adjacency list for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V * V)
O(V * E)
O(E * E)
O(V + E)
explanation: The list stores one entry per vertex plus one entry per edge (two per edge if undirected).

prompt: In a weighted graph, what is the length (cost) of a path?
options: The largest edge weight on the path
The sum of the weights of the edges on the path
The number of cycles the path contains
The number of vertices on the path
explanation: Shortest-path algorithms minimize the total of the edge weights along the path.

prompt: A graph has directed edges A -> B, A -> C, B -> D and C -> D. Which vertex must come first in every topological ordering?
options: D
A
C
B
explanation: A has no incoming edges and must precede B and C, which in turn must precede D.

prompt: In DFS, when does the algorithm backtrack from a vertex?
options: When the vertex has an even degree
When the vertex has no unvisited neighbors left
After visiting exactly two neighbors
As soon as it finds the first neighbor
explanation: A vertex is finished when all its neighbors are visited; DFS then returns to the previous vertex.

prompt: A web crawler starts from one page and must find every page reachable by following links. Which technique does this?
options: Sorting the pages by URL
Graph traversal with BFS or DFS, keeping a visited set
Hashing each page's title
Binary search on the page list
explanation: Following links from a start page is exactly a traversal of the link graph; the visited set prevents loops.

prompt:
What does this BFS print?
from collections import deque
g = {1: [2, 3], 2: [4], 3: [], 4: []}
q, order = deque([1]), []
while q:
    u = q.popleft(); order.append(u)
    q.extend(g[u])
print(order)
explanation: BFS visits 1, then its neighbors 2 and 3, then the neighbor of 2, which is 4. (The second option is a DFS order.)

prompt: How does DFS explore a graph?
options: It only follows edges with the smallest weight
It visits all neighbors of a vertex before going deeper
It visits vertices in sorted order
It goes as deep as possible along a path and backtracks only when it hits a dead end
explanation: DFS keeps moving to an unvisited neighbor and returns to earlier vertices only when none remain.

prompt: In an undirected graph, what is the degree of a vertex?
options: The number of vertices in the whole graph
The number of edges incident to that vertex
The length of the longest path starting at that vertex
The number of cycles passing through that vertex
explanation: Degree counts the edges touching a vertex, which equals its number of neighbors in a simple graph.

prompt: Why does BFS keep a 'visited' set?
options: To count the number of edges
To store the edge weights
To avoid visiting the same vertex repeatedly and looping forever in graphs with cycles
To sort the vertices by degree
explanation: Without marking visited vertices, a cycle would cause the same vertices to be enqueued again and again.

prompt: When is an undirected graph called connected?
options: When it has exactly V - 1 edges
When it contains no cycles
When there is a path between every pair of vertices
When every vertex has at least one self-loop
explanation: Connectivity means any vertex can reach any other; a connected graph may or may not contain cycles.

prompt: What is a weighted graph?
options: A graph in which each edge has an associated numeric value such as cost or distance
A graph that contains at least one cycle
A graph in which every vertex has the same degree
A graph with more edges than vertices
explanation: Edge weights model quantities like distance, time, or cost, and are used by shortest-path algorithms.

prompt: What is the maximum number of edges in a simple undirected graph (no self-loops, no parallel edges) with 4 vertices?
explanation: Each pair of vertices can have at most one edge, so the maximum is C(4,2) = 4*3/2 = 6.

prompt: In a social network where friendship is mutual, how are people and friendships best modeled?
options: People as directed edges and friendships as weights
People as edges and friendships as vertices
People as stack frames and friendships as queues
People as vertices and friendships as undirected edges
explanation: Mutual relationships are symmetric, so undirected edges between person-vertices model them naturally.

prompt: How can the number of connected components of an undirected graph be counted?
options: Sort the vertices and count the distinct labels
Run BFS or DFS from every unvisited vertex and count how many times a new search is started
Count the number of edges and divide by 2
Count the vertices with degree 1
explanation: Each new traversal start discovers one entire component not seen before.

prompt: Which data structure does breadth-first search use to keep track of vertices to visit?
options: A queue
A stack
A binary search tree
A heap ordered by vertex id
explanation: BFS needs first-in, first-out order so that vertices closer to the start are processed first.

prompt: What property does the adjacency matrix of an undirected graph always have?
options: All its diagonal entries are 1
Every row has the same sum
It is symmetric: matrix[i][j] equals matrix[j][i]
Its rows are sorted in increasing order
explanation: An undirected edge between i and j is recorded in both directions.

prompt: A graph is made up of which two components?
options: A set of keys and a set of values
A set of vertices (nodes) and a set of edges connecting them
A set of rows and a set of columns
A set of roots and a set of leaves
explanation: A graph G = (V, E) consists of vertices V and edges E, each edge joining two vertices.

prompt: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting starts by placing which vertices in its queue?
options: Only the vertex with the highest degree
All vertices with out-degree 0
All vertices with in-degree 0
All vertices of the graph
explanation: Vertices with no incoming edges have no prerequisites, so they can safely come first.

prompt: In what order does BFS visit vertices?
options: As deep as possible along one path before backtracking
In increasing order of vertex label
Level by level: all vertices at distance 1 from the start, then distance 2, and so on
In random order
explanation: BFS explores all neighbors of the current level before moving on to the next level.

prompt: A computer network connects routers by cables. If you want to know whether any two routers can communicate, which graph property do you check?
options: Whether the graph is a complete binary tree
Whether the graph is connected (a path exists between them)
Whether the number of routers is prime
Whether every router has exactly two cables
explanation: Two routers can communicate exactly when there is a path between them, i.e. they lie in the same connected component.

prompt: Web pages link to other web pages through hyperlinks. What kind of graph models this?
options: A matrix with only diagonal entries
An undirected graph, because a link always goes both ways
A complete binary tree
A directed graph, where pages are vertices and links are directed edges
explanation: A page A linking to page B does not mean B links back to A, so edges are directed.

prompt: What is the time complexity of BFS on a graph stored as an adjacency list with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V * E)
O(V log V)
O(E²)
O(V + E)
explanation: Each vertex is enqueued once and each edge is examined a constant number of times.

prompt: A recursive DFS in Python is run on a path-shaped graph with 100,000 vertices. What is the most likely problem?
options: The output is sorted incorrectly
DFS silently switches to BFS
A RecursionError, because the recursion depth exceeds Python's default limit
The graph is rejected because it has no cycles
explanation: Recursive DFS uses one stack frame per vertex on the path; Python's default limit is about 1000 frames. An explicit stack avoids this.

prompt: Which algorithm finds the shortest paths from one source vertex in a weighted graph whose edge weights are all non-negative?
options: Dijkstra's algorithm
Kahn's algorithm
Binary search
Breadth-first search, because it always minimizes total weight
explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly settles the closest unsettled vertex and works when no edge weight is negative; BFS only minimizes the number of edges.

prompt: Which representation is usually preferred for a sparse graph (far fewer edges than V*V)?
options: Adjacency matrix
A 3-dimensional array
Adjacency list
Both use the same space
explanation: An adjacency list uses O(V+E) space, whereas a matrix wastes O(V*V) space on missing edges.

prompt: What distinguishes a directed edge (u, v) from an undirected edge between u and v?
options: A directed edge connects three or more vertices
A directed edge can be followed only from u to v
A directed edge always has a weight
A directed edge can only be used once in a path
explanation: Direction means the edge allows travel from u to v but not automatically from v to u.

prompt: A graph has V vertices. What is the size of its adjacency matrix?
options: V x V
E x E
V x E
V x log V
explanation: The matrix has one row and one column per vertex, so V * V cells.

prompt: An undirected graph has edges 0-1, 0-2, and 1-3. Running BFS from vertex 0, at which level (distance from 0) is vertex 3 discovered?
options: Level 0
Level 2
Level 3
Level 1
explanation: Vertex 3 is reached via 0 -> 1 -> 3, which uses two edges.

prompt: An undirected graph has 5 edges. What is the sum of the degrees of all its vertices?
options: It depends on the number of vertices
explanation: Each edge contributes 1 to the degree of each of its two endpoints, so the degree sum is 2 * 5 = 10.

prompt: With an adjacency matrix, how long does it take to check whether an edge between u and v exists?
options: O(V)
O(E)
O(log V)
explanation: The answer is just matrix[u][v], a direct array lookup.

prompt: A graph has directed edges A -> B, B -> C and A -> C. Which sequence is a valid topological ordering?
options: A, B, C
A, C, B
C, B, A
B, A, C
explanation: A, B, C is the only order where A precedes B, B precedes C, and A precedes C; the others each break one edge.

prompt: What is a cycle in a graph?
options: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex
A path that visits every vertex exactly once
A vertex that has no edges
An edge that connects two different components
explanation: A cycle returns to its starting vertex, e.g. A -> B -> C -> A.

prompt: What is a topological ordering of a directed graph?
options: An ordering of the vertices from smallest to largest label
An ordering of the vertices from smallest to largest degree
A linear ordering of the vertices in which, for every edge u -> v, u appears before v
The order in which BFS first visits the vertices
explanation: A topological order respects every edge direction, so each vertex comes after all the vertices that point to it.

prompt: A graph has edges A-B with weight 2, B-D with weight 3, and A-D with weight 10. What is the cost of the cheapest path from A to D?
explanation: The route A -> B -> D costs 2 + 3 = 5, which is cheaper than the direct edge of weight 10.

prompt: What is the time complexity of DFS on a graph stored as an adjacency list with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V * E)
O(V + E)
O(log V)
O(V²)
explanation: Every vertex is visited once and every edge is examined a constant number of times.

What does this code print?
g = {1: [], 2: []}
g[1].append(2)
g[2].append(1)
print(g)
explanation: For an undirected edge the code adds 2 to 1's list and 1 to 2's list.
